source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, the marketplace was a place where the clever merchant won and ordinary people lost. He transformed it entirely by establishing open access, banning sham bidding and hoarding, and creating the hisbah system of market inspectors. Discover how 7th-century marketplace reforms created the foundation for Islamic commercial law. Topics: Medina Marketplace, Hisbah System, Najash, Fair Weights, Consumer Protection, Khiyar Series: Historical Islamic Economics (Part I) • Episode 2 of 6

x.single_post: Most people think market regulation began with modern consumer protection laws. It actually started with a market inspector in Medina in 622 CE.
thread: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, the marketplace was rigged. Clever merchants won. Ordinary people lost.
He transformed it by banning sham bidding, preventing hoarding, and establishing open access for all traders.
The hisbah system appointed market inspectors to ensure fair weights and honest dealing.
We reinvented consumer protection 1,400 years later and called it progress. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-2

linkedin.post: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, he found a marketplace designed for exploitation. Clever merchants used sham bidding, hoarding, and deceptive practices to systematically disadvantage ordinary traders and consumers. His response wasn't just spiritual guidance—it was comprehensive market reform. He established open access, banned najash (artificial price inflation), prevented hoarding, and created the hisbah system: appointed market inspectors who ensured fair weights, honest dealing, and consumer protection. These weren't abstract principles. They were practical regulations that transformed how commerce operated, creating the foundation for Islamic commercial law that would govern trade across continents for centuries. What strikes me is how these 7th-century reforms anticipated modern consumer protection by more than a millennium. The core insight remains unchanged: markets need structure and oversight to serve everyone, not just the clever few. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-2

The same principles we call "consumer protection" today were perfected in 7th-century Arabia. Markets need structure to serve everyone, not just the clever few. Some truths are timeless. short_video.hook: Consumer protection didn't start where you think it did
short_video.voiceover: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, the marketplace was rigged. Clever merchants used sham bidding and hoarding to exploit ordinary people. His solution was revolutionary: ban deceptive practices, ensure open access, establish fair weights, and create market inspectors called the hisbah system. These weren't abstract principles—they were practical regulations that transformed commerce. We spent fourteen hundred years reinventing consumer protection. It was already perfected in seventh-century Arabia.
